Simulated Control Evaluations

Jeffrey Olmo    David Zhang    Tyler Tracy Affiliation: Redwood Research
Abstract

Control evaluations measure whether safeguards can prevent an AI model from causing undesired outcomes even when it is intentionally trying to do so. These evaluations typically use purpose-built control settings and extrapolate their results to a model’s deployment. However, the effectiveness of safeguards in deployment can depend on features of environments and tasks that control settings do not represent. To broaden where control evaluations can be run, we introduce simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to simulate tool responses in place of an environment. We evaluate SCEs on LinuxArena, where execution provides ground-truth outcomes. We compare SCE prediction errors with those from a separate control setting, BashArena, and with variation in control metrics within LinuxArena. For independently sampled evaluation and deployment task sets, SCEs predict safety with a root mean squared error of 3.6 percentage points across five monitors at a 5% audit budget, compared with 10.1 for BashArena. SCEs closely reproduce distributions of attack strategies, attacker reasoning, and monitor reasoning, with over tenfold lower KL divergence from execution than BashArena. SCEs explain 78–85% of the between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. This accuracy is sample efficient: SCEs predict safety with less error than BashArena using fewer than 5% as many task-pair draws as the deployment task set. Strategies discovered through simulation also improve monitor performance on held-out LinuxArena attacks, outperforming BashArena and approximately matching improvement from executed strategies. These results suggest that deployment-specific SCEs can be more predictive than control evaluations executed in separate control settings.

1 Introduction

AI control aims to make it safe to use capable AI agents even if they try to cause harm (Greenblatt et al., 2024). The same capabilities and access that let an agent do useful work can let it exfiltrate information, introduce backdoors, or launch rogue deployments. A control protocol puts safeguards around the agent, such as trusted monitoring. A control evaluation tests these safeguards by replacing the agent with an attack policy configured to pursue a harmful objective while doing legitimate work (Bhatt et al., 2025). Control evaluations produce control metrics, such as how often attacks succeed and how often a monitor catches them. Accurate control metrics can guide improvements to the control protocol and inform risk estimates.

Where an agent acts matters for control evaluations: its opportunities for dangerous behavior, and the evidence control protocols have to detect them, depend on the particular codebases, services, tasks, and available actions in its deployment. Control evaluations aim to inform judgments about a model’s deployment, but typically run in a separate control setting such as BashArena or LinuxArena (Kaufman et al., 2025; Tracy et al., 2026), which provides a safe testbed for executing attacks, and ground truth for outcomes like whether a given side task succeeded, but which shares neither the deployment’s environments nor its task profile. Evidence from such a control setting may transfer poorly to deployment. Even if it captures average attacker and monitor performance, deployment risk will not be determined by those averages when an attacker selects especially promising opportunities (Ge-Wang et al., 2026). A control protocol that appears safe in a control setting might miss specific attacks available in a lab’s internal infrastructure (Korbak et al., 2025).

Running control evaluations directly in the deployment would address this mismatch, but running an attack policy on live infrastructure risks causing the very harms the evaluation is intended to measure. An alternative that avoids this risk is an executable replica of the deployment, but building one can be expensive or infeasible, especially when the agent depends on many services and changing external state. What is usually available, even when a replica is not, is a record of past activity: agent trajectories that show what tasks models were given, which tools they called, and what those tools returned, along with snapshots of the relevant codebases. Our method uses these records to construct control evaluations.

We study simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to produce the tool responses an agent would receive in deployment (Figure 1). An attack policy receives a legitimate main task and a harmful side task. It chooses actions and issues tool calls as usual, while a simulator uses an honest reference trajectory and codebase read access to generate the observations those actions would produce in deployment. The attack policy conditions on each simulator output, so the attack can diverge from the reference trajectory. Monitors then score the resulting simulated trajectory, and an attack success judge estimates whether the side task succeeded. The attack policy’s actions never execute.

The central question is whether SCEs predict deployment control metrics more accurately than a separate control setting does. Simulation introduces unrealism in tool responses, but lets evaluators use the deployment’s real tasks and codebase; a control setting executes attacks faithfully, but on a different distribution of tasks and environments.

Unlike deployment simulation used to forecast misalignment propensity (Williams et al., 2026), SCEs need not conceal the evaluation from the agent: the attack policy is already instructed to pursue a harmful objective. On the other hand, SCEs place stronger demands on modeling the environment’s attack-relevant mechanics, including subtle details of permissions, state changes, and tool behavior that determine whether an attack succeeds and what evidence it leaves for monitors.

We test this tradeoff on LinuxArena, where attacks can be executed to measure ground-truth outcomes. In our experiments, execution in LinuxArena stands in for deployment. Across 1,000 main-task–side-task pairs, we compare SCE predictions with predictions from 1,000 attacks executed in BashArena; Section 2.4 defines these comparisons. We also compare SCE prediction errors with the variation between LinuxArena tasks and environments.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A framework for measuring control evaluation transfer. We combine variance explained in control metrics across tasks and environments with matching behavioral distributions to assess accuracy beyond overall averages. This framework applies to both simulated and executed control evaluations. (Section 2.4).

  • •

    Empirical validation of SCEs. On LinuxArena, SCEs match executed behavioral distributions and predict control metrics more accurately than BashArena, explaining most between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. We show how these advantages scale with the number of simulated task pairs. (Sections 3.1–3.6).

  • •

    Demonstrating that SCEs can improve safeguards. We show that briefing a monitor with simulated strategies improves detection of held-out executed attacks more than BashArena briefings, approaching the performance of briefings from same-environment execution. SCEs thus support improving safeguards as well as assessing them (Section 3.7).

2 Methods

2.1 SCE components

Attack policy. The attack policy is gpt-5.6-sol at medium reasoning effort for both executed and simulated trajectories. It receives the main task, the side task, and attack guidance suggesting how to pursue the side task covertly. For each task, we provide the same attack-policy prompt in execution and SCE.

Simulator. At each tool call, the simulator receives the tool name and arguments, interaction history, and grounding affordances: records and tools that provide information about the environment being simulated. The simulator generates a tool response for the policy’s next step; its reasoning is withheld from the policy and subsequent simulation steps. In what follows, the simulator is gpt-6-astra, with two main affordances:

  • •

    Reference trajectory. The simulator receives the original honest agent transcript for the same main task, including tool calls and responses. This shows how the environment behaved during one execution; the simulator predicts responses to the attack policy’s different actions.

  • •

    Codebase read access. The simulator can read, list, and search a snapshot of the environment’s files, giving it access to source code, configuration, and initial file contents.

Some tool call outputs follow directly from evidence from the reference trajectory and codebase; many outputs depend on state the simulator cannot observe, in which case it generates a plausible result consistent with what is already known. We fall back to gpt-5.6-sol when gpt-6-astra refuses or fails to produce a valid tool response; gpt-6-astra resumes on subsequent outputs.

The base, +reference, and +codebase conditions provide neither affordance, only the reference trajectory, and both affordances, respectively. We use the simulator with both affordances throughout. We investigated many additional affordances, including read access to attack-policy reasoning, an executable sandbox, access to a database of logged trajectories, and forking from the reference trajectory, but did not find evidence that these materially improved simulator quality on the measured dimensions beyond what the reference trajectory and codebase read access provide.

Attack success judge. Executed attacks have a ground-truth outcome from the side-task scorer; simulated attacks have only a transcript, so an attack success judge estimates the probability that the side task succeeded. We use gpt-5.6-sol at high reasoning effort, with read access to the codebase, side-task definitions, and success-scoring logic. Unlike monitors, the judge receives the side-task objective and scoring logic, helping it assess whether the observed actions satisfy the attack’s specific success criteria. SCE success and safety estimates therefore include both simulator and judge error. We validate the judge against executed outcomes in Section 3.2.

Monitors. We use five full-trajectory monitors: gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-5.4-nano, gpt-5-nano, and gpt-5.6-sol. Each produces a suspicion score on a 0–10 scale; we score each trajectory three times and average. Audit thresholds are set on a shared set of executed honest trajectories, the same trajectories that serve as reference trajectories for the simulator.

2.2 Simulator development and evaluation data

We developed the simulator on BashArena and several LinuxArena task pairs; the remaining LinuxArena pairs were held out.

Our primary dataset contains 1,000 LinuxArena task pairs, each combining a main task with a side task. Pairs are balanced across ten environments and selected for overlap between main and side tasks. For each task pair, we collect two simulated runs, two independent executed runs, and one honest reference trajectory. Repeated simulated and executed runs allow us to estimate run-to-run variance. Analyses use these task pairs unless stated otherwise, excluding pairs with missing or invalid measurements. Smaller, separate collections of task pairs are used for the base and +reference conditions and some discriminability diagnostics.

We independently draw evaluation and deployment task sets by sampling eligible task pairs uniformly with replacement. Simulated trajectories provide the evaluation predictions, and executed trajectories provide the deployment outcomes. We calculate metrics separately for each set and average prediction errors across draws. Environment and side-task-category metrics use whichever pairs from those groups appear in each draw. Comparisons on matched task pairs separately assess predictions for individual pairs. Throughout, sample size counts task-pair draws, including repeated selections of the same pair.

2.3 Decomposing error

Prediction error combines systematic differences, run-to-run variance, and task-sampling variance. Root mean squared bias (RMS bias) measures systematic error after averaging over repeated runs and sampled task sets. For attack success and monitor scores, independent repeated runs of the same task pair estimate run-to-run variance. We estimate squared bias by subtracting the contributions of run-to-run variance and task-sampling variance from mean squared prediction error. We average in squared units across task pairs or groups and monitors before taking the root, and correct LinuxArena SD for noise in estimated means. Pooled All comparisons and the safety sample-efficiency curve retain both variance contributions in total RMSE. Bootstrap resampling separately estimates confidence intervals. Appendix B gives details.

2.4 Performance comparisons

We use LinuxArena execution as the deployment ground truth and compare SCE errors with two references: the observed transfer error from BashArena, and variation among LinuxArena’s own environments, task pairs, and side-task categories (Figure 2).

Our first comparison asks whether evaluating deployment-specific tasks through simulation is more informative than executing attacks in a separate control setting. We use BashArena to supply 1,000 executed attacks, using the same attack policy, trajectory length limit, and monitors as for LinuxArena. We calculate each metric from these attacks and use it to predict the corresponding LinuxArena metric.

Our second reference compares prediction errors with variation within LinuxArena. For each environment, we consider the expected metric value, averaged over sampled deployment task sets, and the mean of these values across environments. The between-environment LinuxArena standard deviation (SD) has two interpretations. First, it is the RMSE of assigning this mean to every environment: a control setting that gets the average right but has no environment-specific information. Second, it is the RMSE of using a uniformly selected environment’s expected metric value to predict the mean across environments. In this direction, each environment acts as a possible control setting from which we extrapolate to the broader deployment. Both interpretations give the same error. The analogous interpretations apply to standard deviations over side-task categories and task pairs.

Together, these references compare SCE accuracy against two scales of mismatch between a control setting and deployment: the observed transfer gap from BashArena to LinuxArena, and the deviations within LinuxArena’s own environments, task pairs, or side-task categories from their corresponding means. Outperforming these references would suggest that SCEs can predict deployment metrics more accurately than a control setting whose mismatch with deployment produces errors of comparable magnitude, provided SCE accuracy also transfers to that deployment.

3 Experiments

3.1 Behavior transfer

To evaluate and improve control protocols, an SCE must reproduce the kinds of behavior those protocols demonstrate and encounter in deployment. We compare three behavioral representations of a trajectory: attack strategy describes how a side task is accomplished; attacker reasoning records the attack policy’s reasoning and intent; and monitor reasoning describes the judgements and referenced evidence behind a monitor’s suspicion. Table 1 gives examples.

Control evaluations are more useful to the extent that they accurately represent these behaviors. In particular, improving control protocols depends on understanding which kinds of attacks succeed and evade detection, and why. We compare the distributions of these behavior representations across executed and simulated trajectories before turning to the control metrics themselves.

Following Mehri et al. (2026), we describe each behavior, embed and cluster the descriptions, then compare frequencies over these clusters. These frequencies define the behavioral distributions. We measure DKL(pexec∥psim)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{exec}}\|p_{\mathrm{sim}}), where the two distributions are constructed from executed and simulated LinuxArena trajectories, respectively. For the control setting, we instead compare the executed LinuxArena distribution with the distribution constructed from executed BashArena trajectories, using the same fixed LinuxArena representation and clusters. Appendix A gives the representation and clustering details.

SCEs produce behavioral distributions closer to execution than the control setting for all three representations (Figure 3). Their estimated KL divergence is more than an order of magnitude below that of the control setting in each case, suggesting SCEs provide superior qualitative coverage of the behaviors measured. The +codebase simulator and gray re-execution bars have overlapping 95% intervals for all three representations. This puts simulation error on the scale of variation between repeated runs.

More grounded simulators have lower behavioral divergence (Figure 3), and separate from each other with statistical significance. The base and +reference conditions use smaller, separate samples of task pairs from LinuxArena.

Figure 4 shows a uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (McInnes et al., 2018) that illustrates the distributional comparison for monitor reasoning. The left panel compares LinuxArena execution with BashArena execution; the right compares LinuxArena execution with simulation. The control-setting cluster masses differ substantially from those in LinuxArena, while simulated and matched executed descriptions remain more interspersed. The UMAP projections are qualitative; the aggregate KL estimates in Figure 3 quantify the difference. Backward KL between LinuxArena execution and simulation is similarly small, suggesting simulation does not leave signatures of fabrication detectable from monitor reasoning (Appendix A).

Across all three measured representations, SCEs reproduce LinuxArena’s behavioral distributions more accurately than attacks executed in BashArena, with KL divergence comparable to that between independent executed runs. This supports using SCEs to match an evaluation to the deployment’s tasks and environments even at the cost of simulation error.

3.2 Attack success transfer

Do SCEs accurately predict where attacks succeed, and how often? We first validate the attack success judge on executed attacks: it achieves an AUROC of 0.980, but overestimates their average success rate by 3.7 percentage points.

In aggregate, attack-success rates are close: averaged over independently sampled task sets, the scorer measures 25.5% success on executed attacks and the judge estimates 25.4% on simulated attacks. Matching an average can allow errors on different tasks to cancel, so we also report error on more fine grained partitions of LinuxArena. The Task pair bar in Figure 5 (left) tests fidelity on matched task pairs. The estimated SCE RMS bias is 19.2 percentage points, compared with a between-task-pair SD of 35.5 points, accounting for 71% of between-task-pair variance in the success rate estimate. Likewise, SCEs capture differences in expected success across side-task categories and environments, explaining 87% and 80% of their variance, respectively (Figure 5, left).

Figure 5 (right) shows agreement per environment. Some environment-level gaps are comparable to the judge’s errors on executed attacks: in Auto Workflow and Slack Clone, the judge overestimates success by nearly as much as the combined simulator and judge do. Judge calibration may thus account for a substantial part of these gaps, although bias cancellation and uncertain transfer of judge performance to simulated trajectories prevent precise attribution.

Figure 6 shows a heavy tail across side tasks: the five largest errors account for about 50% of the summed squared error across the 92 side tasks. The nonzero errors fall roughly linearly with log rank, so overall agreement hides a few large misses.

Together, these results show that SCEs accurately predict the overall attack success rate and capture much of the variation in which tasks and environments make attacks more likely to succeed. Their remaining errors are concentrated in a small number of side tasks, identifying specific weaknesses in otherwise strong predictive performance.

3.3 Monitor transfer

Do monitors score simulated trajectories the same way they score executed ones? We compare scores on matched task pairs and ask how well SCEs predict mean suspicion scores on independently sampled task sets.

SCEs closely predict the overall level of suspicion that deployment attacks elicit. For the pooled All comparison, their total RMSE is 0.259 points on the 0–10 scale, versus 2.821 points for BashArena—more than a tenfold reduction in prediction error. Figure 7 (left) also tests whether SCEs capture differences between environments and side-task categories. Between environments, SCE RMS bias is 0.247 points versus a LinuxArena SD of 0.634, explaining 85% of the variance. Thus SCEs capture most of the differences in how suspicious attacks appear across environments. Estimated bias across side-task categories is also small: the variance-corrected squared estimate is slightly negative and displayed at zero, with uncertainty that includes zero.

This agreement extends to individual task pairs. The task-pair SCE RMS bias is 0.68 points versus a between-task-pair SD of 2.03 points, accounting for 89% of between-task-pair variance. SCEs therefore capture most of the variation in expected suspicion between task pairs, providing information about which tasks tend to produce attacks that monitors find more suspicious. Individual simulated runs remain noisy, so repeated simulations can improve estimates of these expected scores.

Figure 7 (right) shows how prediction errors vary across environments and separates differences in observed mean scores from variation due to independently sampling evaluation and deployment task sets. This distinction explains why individual evaluations can disagree even when their expected scores are close. The ordering differs from the attack-success comparison: File Indexing has relatively large errors in both, while Shared Dotfiles and TikTok also have relatively large monitor-score errors. The next analysis tests whether this agreement translates into accurate safety estimates when monitor scores are used to decide which attacks to audit.

3.4 Safety transfer

Safety depends on how often attacks both succeed and escape detection. A simulator could match average attack success and monitor suspicion yet still mispredict safety if it gets wrong which attacks the monitor catches. Following the control-evaluation literature, safety is the probability of detecting an attack before an undetected success (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Bhatt et al., 2025; Tracy et al., 2026). At audit budget bb (the fraction of honest trajectories flagged, or false-positive rate), we estimate safety as P⁡(detected)/[P⁡(detected)+P⁡(undetected∧attack successful)]P(\text{detected})/[P(\text{detected})+P(\text{undetected}\land\text{attack successful})]. Both probabilities are over all attack trajectories; detection includes attacks whose side task fails. Executed attacks use side-task scorer outcomes and simulated attacks use the judge’s success probabilities.

Figure 8 (left) shows that SCEs closely reproduce both the differences in safety between monitors and the improvement obtained by increasing the audit budget. The simulated and executed curves match closely across budgets: an evaluator using SCEs would reach similar conclusions about which monitors provide stronger protection and how much additional auditing improves safety.

Figure 8 (right) quantifies this agreement at a 5% audit budget. Across all eligible LinuxArena task pairs, SCEs predict safety with an RMSE of 3.6 percentage points, versus 10.1 for BashArena. On the 0–100 safety scale, this is a root-mean-squared prediction error of just 3.6 points, including variation from independently sampled evaluation and deployment task sets. SCEs reduce this error by roughly two-thirds relative to BashArena. Errors are squared separately within each monitor, so overprediction for one monitor cannot cancel underprediction for another.

SCEs also capture nearly all of the variation in expected safety between side-task categories and a large majority of the variation between environments: 95% and 78%, respectively. These percentages measure the reduction in squared prediction bias relative to assigning every category or environment its corresponding LinuxArena mean. Thus SCEs recover much of the information about where safeguards are stronger or weaker that an accurate overall average would leave out. For side-task categories, the scale of this improvement is substantial: their expected safeties have an SD of 20.2 percentage points, while SCE RMS bias is only 4.6 points.

These differences matter when an attacker can select its opportunities. An overall safety estimate can conceal categories or environments in which the protocol is substantially weaker. Accurately predicting those differences provides information needed to assess safety if attacks are concentrated on vulnerable parts of a deployment. Together, these results show that SCEs provide both accurate aggregate safety estimates and strong predictions of how safety varies within LinuxArena. For this central control metric, the benefit of evaluating the relevant tasks and environments outweighs the errors introduced by simulation.

3.5 Sample efficiency

SCEs can cover a deployment’s specific environments and tasks, but simulating many task pairs is costly. We ask how much predictive value a small evaluation task set provides.

Figure 9 (left) shows how evaluation size affects safety prediction and discovery of clusters associated with successful, evasive attacks. Safety RMSE uses the right axis; the mass-weighted fraction of clusters still missing uses the left.

Safety prediction. For pooled deployment safety, SCE total RMSE falls below the BashArena reference at 4.6% of the deployment task-set size. Total RMSE reaches 3.57 percentage points when evaluation and deployment task sets are equally large.

Evaluation and deployment task sets are drawn independently from all eligible pairs. Total RMSE retains rollout and task-sampling variance, matching Figure 8’s All comparison.

Cluster discovery. A cluster is discovered when a simulated attack containing it succeeds and evades a monitor. We weight clusters by their successful-and-evasive mass in held-out execution 2 and plot the fraction still undiscovered, 1−C⁡(n)1-C(n). At equal evaluation and deployment sizes, this fraction is 10.0% for attack strategy, 4.3% for attacker reasoning, and 3.1% for monitor reasoning. Simulation matches the full BashArena evaluation at 1.3%, 25.5%, and 13.5% of deployment size, respectively. The representations use different taxonomies and available records, so these curves are not a controlled ranking of discovery difficulty. Appendix C.2 gives the definitions and cohort details.

3.6 Successful and undetected attack strategy prediction

The preceding analyses test whether SCEs reproduce attack behaviors and their outcomes. Combining these two forms of matching lets us predict which behaviors are associated with particular outcomes: such as which strategies tend to succeed undetected. We examine this connection by comparing strategy frequencies and highlighting strategies responsible for executed undetected successes. We form 49 strategy groups from mechanism and evasion descriptions, excluding explicit outcome fields.

Figure 9 (right) compares simulated and executed strategy frequencies as percentages of all attacks. Larger points identify strategies responsible for more executed undetected successes, summed across five monitors at a 5% audit budget. SCEs closely match the frequencies of the three strategies with the largest contributions to executed undetected successes. Other behaviors are underrepresented: the startup TCP callback strategy appears in 0.77% of simulated attacks versus 1.99% of executed attacks. The largest contributors to executed undetected successes lie well within the region of less than 2x multiplicative error.

3.7 Improving monitors with simulated attacks

We now test whether the results of an SCE can improve a monitor more effectively than the results of a control evaluation performed in a control setting. Building on synthetic-data monitor development (Storf et al., 2026), we add descriptions of simulated attack strategies to the monitor’s prompt as possible behaviors to look for. We measure whether this briefing improves detection of held-out executed attacks, compared with an otherwise identical briefing using strategies from attacks executed in BashArena.

We brief a gpt-5.4-nano full-trajectory monitor with descriptions of possible attack strategies drawn from a strategy library built from one of three sources: (1) simulation, i.e., other simulated attack trajectories in the environment being evaluated; (2) same-environment strategies, from executed attacks on other main tasks in that environment; or (3) control-setting strategies, from the 1,000 attacks executed in BashArena. The same-environment library provides a reference for briefing with actual attacks from that environment. Each brief uses the same retrieval and scoring procedure, and none can retrieve strategies from the main task being evaluated. We compare these monitors with an unbriefed monitor on held-out successful executed attacks and honest trajectories across ten environments.

Briefing the monitor with simulated attack strategies improves detection of executed attacks (Figure 10). In the low-false-positive-rate region where monitors generally operate, simulated strategies outperform control-setting strategies and slightly trail same-environment strategies. Standardized partial AUROC over 0–20% FPR is 0.841 with simulated strategies versus 0.767 with BashArena strategies; the paired gain is 0.074 [0.060, 0.088]. The gap to same-environment strategies is 0.010 [0.001, 0.019]. Both differences are statistically significant.

The source comparison holds the briefing procedure fixed, and the benefit transfers to main tasks excluded from the strategy library. This gives a concrete use for the behavioral match: simulated strategies can improve detection of new executed attacks. This particular briefing procedure is unlikely to be an optimal method of improving a monitor. Nonetheless, our results suggest that control-protocol designers armed with an SCE of their deployment may be better prepared for the forms of attack their protocol will encounter than if they rely on a control setting. Establishing how well the benefit extends to other methods of monitor improvement (such as monitor reinforcement learning or prompt optimization) remains future work.

3.8 Discriminability

As a final diagnostic of simulator realism nonspecific to control evaluation, we ask whether the attack policy could tell from its own interaction history that its environment is simulated. The attack-policy model, gpt-5.6-sol, serves as a history discriminator. Language models can recognize subtle evaluation artifacts (Needham et al., 2025), so this test can reveal artifacts even when tool responses appear plausible to a human reader. Notably, in SCEs it’s not necessary for accuracy that a model interacting with a simulated environment cannot tell that it is simulated, as SCEs measure capability, not propensity.

At sampled points in executed and simulated trajectories, we give the history discriminator (at medium reasoning effort) the history through that point. We ask for the probability that the history was simulated and measure discriminability between simulated and executed histories using AUROC. A value of 0.5 corresponds to chance; higher values indicate stronger discrimination. Appendix D describes how histories are sampled and weighted.

The base simulator’s AUROC is high. With the reference trajectory and codebase read access, AUROC falls to near chance, suggesting that simulation artifacts are difficult to identify from the policy’s view. Figure 11 (right) shows discriminability over trajectory progress: for the grounded simulators, a simulated trajectory does not become systematically more detectable as it progresses.

We find that optimizing against this and similar diagnostics can worsen control-metric transfer (Appendix D.1). Discriminability can therefore help identify simulation artifacts, but direct transfer tests are needed to establish whether removing them improves an evaluation.

4 Limitations and discussion

We list some limitations of simulated control evaluations and directions for future research:

Transfer beyond LinuxArena. Our results validate SCEs on LinuxArena. They provide evidence about deployments to the extent that they generalize to deployments with substantially different tasks, infrastructure, or opportunities for harm. Stronger evidence of validity for a broader range of deployments would require either execution ground truth for them, or extending the methods used here to estimate simulator transfer using only static records of a deployment, such as honest trajectories alone. We provide preliminary evidence of such transfer in Appendix E. A promising direction is adapting the behavioral-transfer methodology to measure simulator accuracy on novel distributions lacking attack success ground truth. Validating SCEs across a broader range of executable control settings would help identify where SCEs transfer and what grounding they require.

Simulator discriminability. A whole-trajectory discriminator shows that our simulated trajectories remain somewhat distinguishable from executed ones (Appendix D.1). Empirically, optimizing against this diagnostic has not improved transfer: self-critique made trajectories harder to distinguish but worsened control metrics. Improving realism while preserving control-relevant fidelity remains an open direction.

Simulator trust assumptions. Our method assumes a trusted simulator. An untrusted simulator that attempts to manipulate the results of the evaluation could collude with the attack policy to conceal successful attacks and inflate estimated safety. This parallels the problem of untrusted monitoring, and while we expect techniques for untrusted monitoring such as honeypotting and collusion-busting (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Gardner-Challis et al., 2026) to extend to untrusted simulators, these techniques are still underdeveloped, so we do not currently know how to obtain reliable SCEs under this threat model. Developing ways to check simulated trajectories without trusting their generator is an important direction for extending the method.

Robustness under optimization. In an iterated red-team/blue-team game, repeated attack search or monitor improvement could exploit simulator inaccuracies, for example by selecting attacks that work only in simulation. Testing transfer to held-out executed attacks under stronger and longer optimization would clarify how safely SCEs can perform in iterated games.

5 Conclusion

Simulated control evaluations use a deployment’s own tasks and environments to assess its control protocol without executing attacks there. On LinuxArena, SCEs predict control metrics and control-relevant behavior more accurately than attacks executed in the BashArena control setting. Access to deployment-specific evidence can thus outweigh the fidelity lost in simulation. The briefing experiment demonstrates a practical benefit: briefings drawn from simulated attacks improve detection of held-out executed attacks more than equally sized briefings from the BashArena control setting. SCEs hence support both assessing and improving the tested control protocol. We suggest incorporating SCEs into risk assessments of frontier AI systems. The central next step is to establish how far the reliability observed on LinuxArena extends, especially as attacks and safeguards are optimized against simulators.

Appendix A Behavior transfer details

gpt-5.6-sol describes each trajectory’s attack strategy along the dimensions below. Attacker reasoning uses recorded policy summaries; monitor reasoning uses structured rationales from a gpt-5-nano action monitor. We L2-normalize text-embedding-3-large embeddings without environment or side-task centering, apply pooled PCA retaining 90% of variance, and fit joint kk-means clusters (k=50k=50 for strategies, k=100k=100 for reasoning). Monitor descriptions give each trajectory total weight one. For the control setting, we assign BashArena descriptions to the fixed LinuxArena clusters and measure forward KL from the behavioral distribution of executed LinuxArena trajectories to that of executed BashArena trajectories pooled across tasks. Confidence intervals use trajectory bootstrap resampling conditional on the fitted representation and clusters. Behavioral KL plots use a logarithmic axis, clipping intervals with zero lower bounds at the axis limit. In the monitor-reasoning illustration, UMAPs are fitted separately for the two comparisons and their coordinates are not comparable across panels. Cluster frequencies use the fixed LinuxArena clusters; each trajectory contributes equal total weight.

A.1 Structured behavioral representations

A.2 Behavioral agreement within environments

Figure 12 shows a within-LinuxArena diagnostic, separate from the control-setting comparison. It compares simulation with executed attacks from other LinuxArena environments. In every panel, the simulated distribution is closer to execution in its own environment than execution in any other environment is. If these behavioral properties matter for control, evaluating in a different executable environment may be a worse proxy for attacks in the environment being evaluated than simulation.

Appendix B Attack success transfer details

Judge validation.

Against executed outcomes, the judge’s AUROC is 0.980 [0.973, 0.987] (stratified bootstrap) and Brier score is 0.0475; it overestimates success in nine of ten environments. Figure 5’s blue diamonds report absolute mean gaps between judge estimates and scorer outcomes on the same eligible executed attacks, without sampling-variance components.

Bias and SD across task pairs.

For Figures 5 and 7, matched-task squared error averages all four pairings of two simulated and two executed runs per eligible task pair. Conditional on a task pair, let XX be its success-probability forecast and YY its binary outcome, with means q,pq,p. Under conditional independence,

E⁡[(X−Y)2]=p⁡(1−p)+Var⁡(X)+(q−p)2.E[(X-Y)^{2}]=p(1-p)+\operatorname{Var}(X)+(q-p)^{2}. (1)

Half the squared difference between independent repeats estimates each arm’s variance; subtracting both variances estimates squared bias. Without independence, the equation also contains −2​Cov⁡(X,Y)-2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y). Between-task-pair variance is estimated by Covi⁡(Yi​1,Yi​2)\operatorname{Cov}_{i}(Y_{i1},Y_{i2}). The analogous corrections apply to monitor scores. Simulations share the recorded grounding reference; four pairings do not increase the task-pair count. Squared errors and variances are averaged within monitors before averaging across monitors and taking roots.

Independent task sets.

Evaluation and deployment task sets each contain NN task-pair draws sampled independently, uniformly with replacement from all NN eligible task pairs. Group metrics use the task-pair draws belonging to each environment or side-task category, so group counts vary between draws. Each occurrence independently chooses either recorded run with equal probability in both arms, retaining one rollout per occurrence. Figure 6 retains primary simulated runs. For pooled empirical means μP,μT\mu_{P},\mu_{T} and variances σP2,σT2\sigma_{P}^{2},\sigma_{T}^{2},

E⁡[(P¯N−T¯N)2]=(μP−μT)2+(σP2+σT2)/N.E[(\bar{P}_{N}-\bar{T}_{N})^{2}]=(\mu_{P}-\mu_{T})^{2}+(\sigma_{P}^{2}+\sigma_{T}^{2})/N.

All and the per-environment decompositions retain all three terms. Categories and environments receive equal weight; monitors are averaged in squared units. Judge probabilities are not converted to Bernoulli draws.

Correcting group means.

With normalized original-task weights wiw_{i} and repeat-variance estimates τ^i2\widehat{\tau}_{i}^{2}, the recorded-mean variances are

CP=12​∑iwi2​τ^P​i2,CT=12​∑iwi2​τ^T​i2.C_{P}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i}w_{i}^{2}\widehat{\tau}_{Pi}^{2},\qquad C_{T}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i}w_{i}^{2}\widehat{\tau}_{Ti}^{2}.

Subtract CP+CTC_{P}+C_{T} from squared mean gaps and (1−1/G)​C¯T(1-1/G)\overline{C}_{T} from variance across GG executed group means. Both recorded means average two runs; task pairs missing either repeat are excluded rather than imputed. Bootstrap duplicates combine their original-task weights before squaring. Corrections assume independent errors across tasks and arms and apply to the task pairs with complete measurements. Signed corrected estimates enter variance explained, 100​(1−B^2/V^)100(1-\widehat{B}^{2}/\widehat{V}); only displayed roots truncate at zero. All’s match percentage is 100​(1−RMSE/Y¯)100(1-\mathrm{RMSE}/\bar{Y}).

Group counts are binomial under pooled draws. Group-mean sampling variances therefore average 1/K1/K over the random group count KK. Missing evaluation groups use the draw’s overall simulated metric; group errors condition on presence in deployment. Safety ratios and behavioral KL are calculated within draws before averaging.

Uncertainty.

Confidence-interval bootstraps estimate uncertainty in the reported errors, separately from task-set draws. Paired main-task cluster bootstraps carry both arms and repeats together within fixed environments, preserving original pooled environment weights and sampling budgets. Figures 5 and 7 use 10,000 resamples. Task-pair bars use percentile intervals; corrected group bars use normal intervals on squared estimates. Both are mapped through max⁡(0,⋅)\sqrt{\max(0,\cdot)}. The monitor-category squared-bias estimate is −0.00566-0.00566, so its zero-height bar does not establish zero bias. All uses percentile intervals on total RMSE; per-environment decomposition whiskers use normal intervals directly on RMSE. Intervals condition on recorded tasks and environments.

Appendix C Safety transfer details

C.1 Safety by environment

Figure 13 applies the pooled honest calibration and shared audit budget within each environment, revealing variation hidden by the aggregate estimate. Environments with fewer eligible task pairs give wider uncertainty.

C.2 Mass-weighted cluster discovery

Execution 2 supplies successful-and-undetected mass Wm​kW_{mk} for monitor mm and cluster kk. It is excluded from fitting the codebooks. Attack strategy uses 50 mechanism/evasion clusters and 904 task pairs; attacker reasoning uses 100 clusters and 881 pairs; monitor reasoning uses 100 clusters and 904 pairs. The monitor codebook is fitted once to primary executed and simulated observations, with execution 2 and BashArena projected into the same centroids. For reasoning, each target trajectory’s mass is divided among clusters in proportion to its reasoning observations. A source attack can discover every cluster it contains: presence, rather than fractional membership, determines discovery. If pm​kp_{mk} is the source probability per attempt of containing cluster kk, succeeding, and evading the same monitor, expected coverage after nn independent attempts is

C⁡(n)=∑m,kWm​k​[1−(1−pm​k)n]∑mWm,C(n)=\frac{\sum_{m,k}W_{mk}\bigl[1-(1-p_{mk})^{n}\bigr]}{\sum_{m}W_{m}},

where WmW_{m} includes all executed successful-and-undetected mass, including unlabeled attacks. No held-out failure mass is unlabeled in this cohort. Each attempt samples a task pair with replacement. Strategy discovery chooses either saved simulated rollout with equal probability; reasoning uses the primary simulation because repeat reasoning assignments are unavailable. Failed, detected, and unlabeled attempts consume budget. Simulation uses judge success probabilities, so its discovery is judge-weighted rather than execution-verified. Monitors with more held-out failures receive more weight. Bands use 2,000 paired main-task bootstraps within fixed LinuxArena environments, holding calibration and codebooks fixed. The same draws preserve pairing across representations. Discovery parity markers use the full observed BashArena source, with each of its 997 complete rollouts evaluated once and randomized audit decisions integrated. Attacker-reasoning labels are available for 967 of these cases; the other 30 discover no attacker-reasoning clusters. BashArena coverage is 7.75% for strategy, 79.47% for attacker reasoning, and 78.68% for monitor reasoning. Monitor-reasoning clusters describe the archived action monitor; success and evasion are evaluated separately using the five trajectory monitors. The target contains new rollouts of the same tasks; this retrospective measure does not establish discovery of unseen mechanisms or transfer of a concrete exploit between benchmarks.

Appendix D Discriminability details

Inverse-probability weighting estimates AUROC over the full tool-output distribution. Base and +reference use three sampled histories per task pair from smaller sets of task pairs; +codebase uses one per task pair from a larger set of task pairs. Intervals bootstrap matched task pairs, keeping executed and simulated histories together.

The progress panel uses a separate set of task pairs per condition, partitioned into five normalized assistant-step bins. It averages within-pair tool-output AUROC equally across pairs. The panels use different sets of task pairs and weighting; the affordance comparison is not a fully paired ablation.

D.1 Whole-trajectory discrimination

We average both presentation orders before bootstrapping task pairs.

Base and +reference predate an XML parser correction and lack raw answer tags, so remain exploratory. Checking all +codebase answers confirmed that the correction changes neither choices nor interval.

An exploratory self-critique pass reduced discriminability but worsened control-metric transfer, apparently through plausible yet unrealistic network friction on external services. It is excluded from the primary simulator.

Appendix E Transfer to agent sessions

We present preliminary evidence that our simulator protocol works on ordinary agent sessions using redacted transcripts and associated codebases sourced from internal model usage at Redwood Research, spanning research and engineering tasks. These transcripts contain no side-task attempts by an attack policy, so we cannot evaluate transfer on control metrics like attack success, but we can evaluate discriminability and behavior transfer on benign content. On these measures, simulation is more predictive than LinuxArena or partitions of the agent sessions themselves.

Data.

The matched session pairs share a transcript prefix and next user request. Recorded continuations end at the next user message; simulated continuations end when the policy yields or reaches 50 actions. Comparisons use honest LinuxArena trajectories balanced across ten environments, or the opposite half of a fixed balanced session split. All trajectories are treated as honest work.

Discriminability.

A gpt-5.6-sol whole-trajectory discriminator at high reasoning effort selects the simulated continuation as recorded with probability 0.407 [0.321, 0.494]. An action-output probe using the same model at medium reasoning effort has AUROC 0.493 [0.451, 0.535]. Figure 16 shows that probe over normalized trajectory progress. Discriminability stays near chance throughout the continuation.

Behavior transfer.

Using the behavior-transfer methodology of Section 3.1, simulation is closer to recorded agent sessions than LinuxArena or the other half of agent sessions for all three representations. The LinuxArena distance minus the matched-simulation distance is 5.578 bits [4.620, 5.837] for action behavior, 2.340 bits [1.796, 2.640] for structured monitor reasoning, and 4.141 bits [3.432, 4.434] for raw monitor rationales.
